blocks.content: In SolTrace, a snapshot of an optical system in time is considered a “scene”. Previous verisons of SolTrace relied on “stages” to break up the total scene into subsets of geometry. Rays would progress from stage to stage until they either were absorbed or exited the scene.  However, based on feedback, stages can complicate initial user experience. Additionally, stages can result in duplicated geometry in various stages and/or missing ray interactions due to poor stage modeling practices. The original motivation behind the stage concept was to employ efficient tracing and therefore save processing time and allow for a modular representation of a system. Stages can reduce the computational burden for scenes where geometry is sparse (e.g., a small group of heliostats that are a great distance from the receiver).

In the past decades, computer graphics algorithms (e.g., bounding volume hierarchy (BVH)) have made significant improvements to quickly identify a subset of surfaces to test for ray intersections. These algorithms have made it possible to remove SolTrace's legacy method of stages while maintaining computational efficiency. Elemenating stages reduces the modeling burden on the user while also reducing the chances of introducing staging modeling errors.

A scene is comprised of “elements”. Each element consists of a surface, an optical interaction type, an aperture shape and a set of optical properties. The location and orientation of elements are defined within the global coordinate system. SolTrace defines the right-hand global coordinate system as the X-axis points to the east, the Y-axis points to the north, and the Z-axis points to the zenith.

Element interaction type can be defined as either reflection or refraction by using the specified reflectance or transmittance to determine if a ray is reflected or transmited by the surface, respectively. Rays that are not reflected or transmited are absorbed by the surface. Legacy SolTrace had a the capability to model “virtual” stages. Since stages have been removed, the proposed alternative is to defined optical properties of a virtual element where the interaction type is refraction, transmittance is 1, and the front and back index of refraction is 1. This set of optical properties result in a element that does not physically interact with the rays.  Virtual elements are useful for determining ray locations and directions at various positions along the optical path without physically affecting ray trajectory. Each element is defined by a local coordinate system where the aperture is parallel to the X-Y plane.

Before the trace, sun plane boundaries are calculated by project each element bounding box along the sun vector. During the trace, sun rays are generated from the sun plane and then traced sequentially through scene.
